name: setState(updater)
desc: Computes the next state from the latest queued value instead of the value captured by the current render.
body:
The plain form `setCount(count + 1)` reads `count` from the current render. Two calls in one handler both compute the same number, so the state grows by one. The updater form receives whatever is queued when React runs it.

Use it for counters, queues, toggles inside loops, and any callback that may run after the render that created it. The function must be pure: no setters, no requests, no logging of business events. React may call it twice in development to check.

name: useState(initializer)
desc: Passes a function so the initial value is computed on mount only, not on every render.
body:
The argument to `useState` is ignored after the first render, but an expression is still evaluated before the hook sees it. That means `useState(expensive())` pays the cost on every render for a value that is discarded.

Passing a function defers the work. `useState(() => expensive())` is called once per mounted component. If you only need the value, a function is all you keep, and the same rule applies to `useReducer`'s third argument.

name: batched updates
desc: React groups setter calls made in the same tick into a single render.
body:
Batching means the intermediate states are never painted. It also means the state variables keep their old values until the handler returns, so reading `saving` right after `setSaving(true)` gives `false`.

React 18 batches in promises, timeouts and native listeners too. An `await` splits the batch, because by the time the promise resolves the handler has returned. That split is often what you want for a progress flag.

name: state snapshot
desc: Each render gets its own fixed state and props; a setter affects the next render, not the running one.
body:
Treat every render as a photograph: props, state and the handlers created in it hold that moment. The next render is a new photograph with new values.

This explains two common questions. Why does a timer log an old value? Because the callback was created in an old render. Why does reading state right after a setter show the old value? Because the setter schedules a render instead of editing the current one.

name: setState({ ...state, field })
desc: Replaces a state object with a copy, because React state is not merged for you.
body:
Unlike a class component's `setState`, the hook does not merge keys. `setForm({ first_name: 'Anna' })` drops the email and the last name.

The computed key `[field]` keeps one handler for many inputs. It is safe as long as the field name comes from your code, never from user input, and the field exists in the state shape.

name: nested state update
desc: Copies each level of a nested object that lies on the path to the changed field.
body:
Only the path from the root to the changed field needs a fresh object. Copying the whole tree with `JSON.parse(JSON.stringify(x))` loses `undefined`, turns dates into strings and costs time proportional to the data.

Past two levels the spreads hide intent. At that point either flatten the state (`city`, `street` as separate fields) or move it to `useReducer`, where the update gets a name.

name: remove from state array
desc: Builds a new array without the item instead of mutating the old one.
body:
`splice` and `push` mutate the array React already holds. The reference stays the same, the render is skipped, and the old render's data changes under it.

Use `filter` to remove, `map` to replace one item, spread to add. `sort` and `reverse` also mutate, so copy first: `setItems([...items].sort(byName))`.

name: update one state array item
syntax: setItems(items => items.map(i => i.id === id ? { ...i, done: !i.done } : i))
desc: Replaces a single object inside an array while leaving the other items untouched.
body:
The unchanged rows keep their identity, which helps memoized children skip work. Return the original object for every row that is not the target, never a fresh copy of it.

If the array is large and updates are frequent, index the rows by id in a `Map` outside the render, or move the collection into `useReducer` so the update rule lives in one place.

name: reset state with key
desc: Remounts a component when the record changes, so its internal state starts from the initial value.
body:
Changing `key` makes React unmount the old instance and mount a new one. The `useState(customer.first_name)` initial value runs again with the new prop. No effect, no comparison, no stale draft.

This beats the alternative of copying the prop into state and syncing it in `useEffect`, which renders once with the old value and can overwrite edits. Use a value that is stable and unique per record, not an index.

name: derived value in render
syntax: const total = items.reduce((sum, i) => sum + i.price * i.qty, 0)
desc: Computes a value from existing state during render instead of storing and syncing it.
body:
A stored copy starts correct and drifts the first time an update path forgets to refresh it. An effect that syncs the copy adds a render and a moment where the screen shows a number that does not match the list.

Wrap the calculation in `useMemo` only when it is measurably slow or when its identity is passed to a memoized child. For a filter over a few hundred rows, plain code is faster and easier to read.

name: lift state up
desc: Moves shared state to the closest common parent and passes the value down with a change handler.
body:
Two components cannot each own the same fact. Move it to their nearest common parent, pass the value down as a prop, and pass a function down so children can report what happened. Data flows one way and there is one place to debug.

Do not lift by default. State used by one component belongs there. Lifting to the top of the tree turns a keystroke into a render of everything below.

name: controlled field
desc: Binds an input to state so React is the single source of the displayed value.
body:
The input shows what the state says. Typing fires `onChange`, the handler stores the string, and the next render paints it back. Because the value flows from state, validation, formatting and reset all work in one place.

An input with `value` and no `onChange` is read-only and logs a warning. An input with `defaultValue` is uncontrolled, so state updates cannot change what it shows.

name: number input state
desc: Converts the string from a number input and guards against an empty or invalid field.
body:
Every input event carries a string, even when `type="number"`. Storing the string works until you compare or add it. `"2" + 1` gives `"21"`.

`Number('abc')` is `NaN`, and an input bound to `NaN` warns. The `|| 0` turns both `NaN` and an empty string into zero, and `Math.max` keeps the value from going negative through the spinner. Clamp in the handler so the state shape stays clean for the rest of the app.

name: form state as one object
desc: Keeps many fields in one object and updates them through each input's name attribute.
body:
One handler for every field removes a row of near identical functions. The `name` attribute must match a key in the state object, and the key must already exist in the initial object.

This shape is the natural entry point for `useReducer`, because adding validation and a submit status to the same object quickly outgrows a single setter.

name: toggle boolean state
desc: Flips a boolean through the updater form so rapid clicks each see the last value.
body:
For a single click `setOpen(!open)` is correct and shorter. The updater form earns its place when the same handler runs more than once before a render, or when the handler was created in an older render and captured an older `open`.

Keep the boolean itself in state, not a string like `"open"` and `"closed"`. The toggle logic then lives in one expression, and the JSX condition is a plain `open && ...`.
